title: Priyanka and Toys
directAnswer: Each container can hold all toys whose weights lie in a window `[w, w + 4]` for some chosen base weight `w`. To minimise the number of containers, sort the weights ascending and greedily open a new container at the smallest uncovered weight; it then covers everything up to that weight + 4. Skip every toy within the window and repeat at the next uncovered toy. O(n log n) from the sort.

remember.pattern: Greedy interval covering: anchor each window at the smallest uncovered point
remember.formula:
sort weights ascending
units = 0
last = -infinity
for w in weights:
    if w > last + 4:        # not covered by the current window
        units += 1
        last = w             # open a new window [w, w + 4]
return units
rules: A single container covers a contiguous weight window of size 4: any toys with weight in `[w, w + 4]` for the chosen base `w`.
Sort ascending so you always meet the smallest uncovered toy first.
Anchor each new window at that smallest uncovered toy `w`; it greedily covers up to `w + 4`.
Use `w > last + 4` (strictly greater) — a toy exactly at `last + 4` is still inside the window.
Each container is unlimited in count and weight; the only limit is the 4-unit spread of weights it holds.
whenToUse: Cover all points on a line with the fewest fixed-width intervals
Each interval can be positioned freely but has a fixed reach
Sorting reveals that anchoring at the leftmost uncovered point is optimal
Minimising the count of groups, each spanning a bounded range
antiSignals: Intervals have fixed positions you cannot move → interval scheduling, not covering
Capacity is by count or total weight, not by spread → bin packing / knapsack
The window width varies per container → different DP
You must maximise coverage under a fixed number of intervals → a different objective
remember.takeaway: Minimum fixed-width interval cover of points on a line: sort, then greedily anchor each interval at the leftmost uncovered point and jump past its reach. Anchoring at the smallest uncovered point is provably optimal — it covers the most while wasting none of the window to the left.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reframe 'fewest containers' as 'fewest fixed-width intervals covering all points', sort, and anchor greedily — plus getting the inclusive boundary (w + 4) right.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Centering the window on a weight instead of anchoring at the smallest uncovered one, or using `>=` so a toy exactly at the boundary spawns an unnecessary container.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Give the exchange argument: anchoring the window at the leftmost uncovered toy dominates any later anchor, since moving the anchor left never loses coverage and may gain it.

problemStatement:
Priyanka must distribute `n` toys into containers. Each toy `i` has a weight `w[i]`. A single container can hold any number of toys, as long as the **difference between the maximum and minimum weight** of the toys it holds is **at most 4** — i.e. all its toys fit in some window `[base, base + 4]`.

Return the **minimum number of containers** needed to hold all the toys.
constraints: A container holds toys whose weights span at most 4 units (inclusive)
understanding: Picture each toy's weight as a point on a number line. A container is an interval of width 4 that you may slide anywhere; it covers every toy point inside it. We want the fewest such intervals to cover all points. Sorting the points and greedily placing each interval starting at the leftmost uncovered point gives the minimum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the window boundary inclusive — does [w, w+4] include w+4?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A toy at exactly w + 4 is within range (difference of 4 is allowed). Use `> last + 4` to start a new window, not `>=`.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there a limit on how many toys or how much total weight a container holds?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The only constraint is the 4-unit spread between the lightest and heaviest toy in the container.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can weights repeat?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Duplicates simply fall inside the same window and cost nothing extra.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need the actual assignment or just the count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the minimum number of containers. The greedy still implicitly defines a valid assignment if asked.

Sorted [1,2,3,4]. Anchor at 1 covers [1,5], which includes 2,3,4. One container.
Each gap exceeds 4: anchor 10 covers ≤14 (misses 20), anchor 20 covers ≤24 (misses 30), anchor 30. Three containers.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Anchoring Windows at Every Subset
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to acknowledge the search space, then collapse it with sorting.
hints: A solution chooses a set of window anchors so that every toy lies in some [anchor, anchor + 4]. Without insight, you might search over which toys start windows.
Try every subset of toys as potential window starts, check that the chosen windows cover all toys, and keep the smallest valid subset.
There are 2ⁿ subsets — only feasible for tiny n. It exists purely to motivate sorting and the leftmost-anchor greedy.
approaches.complexityReasoning: 2ⁿ candidate anchor subsets, each checked for full coverage in O(n). Exponential and unusable beyond small n.
approaches.explanation:
Imagine deciding, for every toy, whether it 'starts' a container window. Any chosen set of starts defines windows `[w, w + 4]`; the set is valid if every toy lies inside at least one window. Search all `2ⁿ` subsets and keep the smallest valid one.

**Why it's correct.** Every possible placement of windows is considered (a window only ever needs to start at some toy's weight — starting between toys wastes reach), so the minimum valid subset is the true answer.

**Why it's hopeless.** `2ⁿ` subsets is exponential; even `n = 30` is a billion. The constraint allows `n = 100000`, so this never runs.

**The structure it reveals.** Notice a window never benefits from starting to the *left* of the smallest toy it must cover — that just wastes reach. So the optimal anchors are always *toys themselves*, processed left to right, each new window opened exactly at the next uncovered toy. That observation removes the search entirely.
approaches.insight: A window should always be anchored at an actual uncovered toy (anchoring earlier wastes its 4-unit reach). That single observation turns a 2ⁿ subset search into a left-to-right sweep.

dryRun.intro: Try subsets of anchors; the smallest valid one wins. (Sorted [1,2,3,4].)

java.line: if (w[j] >= w[b] && w[j] <= w[b] + 4) covered[j] = true;
java.explanation: A toy is covered if it lies in the window [anchor, anchor + 4].
Track the fewest anchors that cover everything.

python.explanation: Try every anchor subset, smallest sizes first.
First fully-covering subset of this size is the minimum.

pitfalls: Anchoring windows between toys wastes reach and never helps.
Forgetting the boundary is inclusive (w + 4 is covered).

approaches.name: Greedy — Sort and Sweep Fixed-Width Windows (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'open a container at the smallest leftover toy and skip everything within 4 of it'.
hints: Sort the weights ascending. The smallest toy must be in some container — anchor that container's window at it so it reaches as far right as possible.
That window covers everything up to (smallest weight + 4). Skip all those toys; they cost nothing more.
The next uncovered toy forces a new container. Repeat. Count how many containers you open.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n) and dominates; the single sweep is O(n) with only two scalar variables → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort ascending. Sweep left to right. Keep the upper bound `last + 4` of the current container's window (start with `last = −∞`). When a toy's weight exceeds `last + 4`, it can't fit the current window, so open a new container anchored at this toy and set `last` to its weight. Count the opens.

**Why anchor at the smallest uncovered toy — the exchange argument.** The leftmost uncovered toy `w` must go into *some* container, whose window is `[base, base + 4]` with `base ≤ w`. Slide that window right until `base = w`. Since every other uncovered toy is `≥ w`, raising `base` to `w` never drops a toy that was already inside (those toys were `≥ base` and now still `≥ w` only if... ) — more precisely, the window `[w, w + 4]` covers at least as many of the *remaining* (uncovered, hence `≥ w`) toys as any window with `base < w`, because the only toys a lower `base` could additionally cover are `< w`, and there are none left. So anchoring exactly at the smallest uncovered toy is never worse; it covers the longest possible prefix of the remaining toys. Each greedy container therefore covers a maximal run, and any optimal solution can be transformed into this one without increasing the count.

**Why the strict `>` boundary.** A toy at exactly `last + 4` differs from the anchor by 4, which is allowed, so it stays in the current window. Using `>=` would wrongly open a new container for it.

**Why sorting is required.** The argument 'all remaining toys are ≥ the anchor' only holds if we process in non-decreasing order. Without sorting, a later small toy could appear and break the prefix-covering logic.
approaches.insight: Minimum cover by fixed-width intervals = sort + leftmost-anchor sweep. The reusable kernel: when intervals can slide freely, always anchor the next one at the leftmost uncovered point — it dominates every other placement on the remaining points.

pitfalls: Using `>=` instead of `>` — splits a toy that is exactly 4 away into its own container.
Forgetting to sort — the leftmost-anchor argument fails on unsorted input.
Re-anchoring at every toy instead of only uncovered ones — overcounts containers.

commonMistakes: Not sorting the weights before sweeping.
Using a `>=` boundary so a toy exactly 4 units away triggers an extra container.
Centering the window on a weight instead of anchoring at the smallest uncovered toy.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong boundary comparison
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A toy at exactly last + 4 has a weight difference of 4, which is allowed. Using >= opens an unnecessary container.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to sort
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The greedy relies on always seeing the smallest uncovered toy first. Unsorted input breaks the prefix-covering guarantee.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int units = 0; long last = Long.MIN_VALUE;
for (int weight : w) { if (weight > last + 4) { units++; last = weight; } }

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Anchoring on a fixed window grid
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Snapping windows to multiples of 5 (e.g. [0,4],[5,9],…) can split a tight cluster across two containers, overcounting.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: units = len({weight // 5 for weight in w})  # fixed grid buckets
